It happened because the rating-system is thoroughly broken - or more
correctly, it's not made for handling a multiplayer environment.

I suggested earlier that now is a golden opportunity to change it
slightly as we now have the system with Game Wins. Keep the
algorithm, it's more than well-proven (standard issue international
chess-rating).

The one big, and I admit, it's big, disadvantage is that current
ratings may need to be reset, but I actually don't think so.

Suggestion in concrete terms:

If a table creates a Game Win then everyone looses against the person
getting the Game Win.

If a table doesn't create a Game Win then everyone draws.

That's it, nothing else, no comparision between second and third place
and you only win when according to the new rules you actually Game Win.

The difference from today is that bad seating, bad luck, bad breath
and bad mana in general should cost you a maximum of aprox 30 points
during any one game. It also reflects the rules of the game better
as there really (at a five player table) should be one winner and
four loosers.

Sten During

In a hockeygame the team who scores (VP) most wins (gets
on Game Win), and the game may end up as a tie (half a
Game Win to each team (yes, I'm aware that most leagues
use zero, one or two points for loss, tie and win)).
These scores minus the amount of scores a team has
allowed opposing teams to do is totalled in order to
calculate tiebreakers.
At any time during a league when two teams have the same
amount of Game Wins then difference in scores (in this
example effectively VP) is used as tiebreaker. If still
tied then, depending on league, for example most scores
made is used as yet another tiebreaker. This could with
some imagination be compared to TP.

All in all, it's my honest belief that a ratingsystem
based only on Game Wins is to be preferred.

This is an argument for doing away with tournaments altogether (since
according to the argument, the game's multi-player aspect removes its
value as a test of player skill). It is not an argument for your
proposed rating system as much as it is an argument against either of
the rating systems.

I think your arguments may support a different rating system, but
one that is not likely to be implemented due to the increased
bookkeeping required:

NON-OFFICIAL ALTERNATE RATINGS SYSTEM

Victory Points are tracked as a "win" for the recipient against a
"loss" by the player being ousted.

The standard Elo formula is applied only to those pairs.

Example: A B C and D are seated in that order around a table. A
ousts B then ousts C and then ousts D. A receives a "win" against
each other player and each other player receives a "loss" against
A. No other comparisons are made. (This matches your proposal
above, but only for sweeps).

Example: A ousts B then C. Then D ousts A. Score:
A > B
A > C
D > A

Where "X > Y" means X and Y are considered "paired" for Elo rating,
with X receiving the win and Y receiving the loss.

The system would be trivially extended for time-out conditions:
All players left standing (not ousted) when time is called are
rated pairwise against each other as tied.

Example: A ousts B and then time is called.
A > B
A : C
A : D
C : D

You could then track a withdrawal as a tie against every other
player still standing at the time of withdrawal, or just ignore
it.

You would also have to decide whether to apply the Elo ratings
changes instantly at each VP, or to track the "delta VP" based
on game-start ratings at each VP and apply the deltas at the
end (the way the current system does).

The final piece of the puzzle would deal with VP-stealing (via,
for example, Life Boon). You could track that only from the
person being ousted to the recipient, or you could track it
through the player who is the victim of the Life Boon. I think
the latter is more appropriate, but more cumbersome as well.

Anyway, this whole system adds complication to the rating system
in that specific VP "movement" (as seen from the model where each
player brings a VP to the table to be given away when she is
ousted.)

It more adequately achieves the result you're arguing toward, I
think.

"Add?" Just "add"? I think you're missing the point about the ratings
system being zero sum. If you just start adding points without going out
and robbing them from someone else, then it starts to reward people merely
for participating (i.e. you get the opportunity to be in the final). This
opens up the system to a whole slew of implications that a closed zero
sum game doesn't have: mainly, that being able to be in as many tournaments
as possible becomes a ratings boon. (Even the players who don't get to
and finals at all get rewarded, since they frequently get to play players
who've been in the final, which is a ratings boon, too.) I say, "Well,

they don't actually rate people.

slowly increased from the 3000 that people start with. So now people
start with the average number of points but next year, it will be somewhat
less than average. 10 years from now it will likely be much less than
average. Strange stuff.

their little gold stars for participating and winning things, let's do it
blatantly like the original DCI rating system for Magic before they
started using the current one: 10 points for showing up, double the points
for advancing to each subsequent round. That was for a single elimination
tournament. Our round-robin preliminaries would probably be more like
10 points for playing each round and 10 points for each victory point
scored therein. 50 for going to the finals and 50 more for each victory
point scored there. And at the end of the year, you total them, send the
point leaders a plaque (and an invitation to the Continental Tournament of
their choice) and wipe the points clean and start over.

My issue with the current system is that it's far too weighted towards
recent results in comparison to previous rankings. Jyhad frequently
produces results which buck the trend in terms of skill - due to seating
order, bad vs. good luck in the draw of the cards, metagame choices and
so forth. As a result, skillful players can't run their ratings above
a certain level before an unlucky defeat (or several) by someone ranked
much lower chops them back down towards average.

It may be that this can still be arranged through the Elo system.
Having looked at the system, I would say that the problem - and what
therefore likely needs changing - is is the calculation of how many
points are won and lost by each pair of players based on the difference
in their current rating. Right now, a player gets 3300 rating and he
just gets kicked far too hard if he doesn't beat everyone else he plays,
which he's never going to do. So no one can hold a high rating for long.
The solution is to reduce the effect of the difference in ratings points
has on the calculation of win probability, and therefore how many points
get added if the high-rated player wins vs. how many get subtracted if
he loses. Apparently, the ratio of 32 points as the coefficient to 400
as the divisor of the difference in ratings of the exponent of 10 in the
overall divisor (just go look at appendix A if you really want to know(!))
is too high. I'd set the latter number to 1000 or so (a pure intuitive
guess here; it could probably stand someone doing some calculations to
see how it worked out) so that players' ratings could range a lot higher
and lower before differences in ratings made it a lot harder for them
to gain points (if high rated) or lose point (if low rated). It would
still take time to run your rating very high (since the 32 doesn't
change) or very low, but Jyhad being the type of game it is, I would
argue that this is justified and how things have to be.

Comments?

This statement is either circular or wrong: if you mean, the current system
is having this effect because that's the effect the current system - given
the various constants they're choosing to use - has, that would be circular
logic, what Mathematicians term a "tautology". If you mean this is the only
result that can be achieved using ELO, I disagree. Change the constants,

I disagree. That's not really a problem. You just change the constants
to account for the fact that any one recorded result is subject to large
amount of random luck. The system works fine, it just requires different
constants to tune down the effect of any single result. Since each game
turns in 6 (for a four-player game) or 10 (for a five-player game) results,
this is not a problem. It just means it will take the highest and lowest
rated players more games to get to their natural ratings then the current
system, which is completely fair and appropriate.

> and by ranking list I mean the ordered list starting with the tournament
>winner and going downwards.

1) It's not really a problem.

2) There's no way to be perfect in this respect.

I think you're trying to claim that no system will ever work right unless
the ratings system perfectly mirrors the tournament incentives. On some
super-anal-retentive level, that's slightly true but I don't see a real
substantial issue here. If there was, the situation before the Game Wins
rule was even worse: players had an incentive to limit how many victory
points they tried to get in a single game in order to assure themselves
of a minimum number of victory points. This was why the Game Wins rule
was created: players weren't attempting to do the best they possibly could
in a single game. They were sacrificing their chances of doing fantastically
well in favor of more security about getting the minimal number of victory
points to qualify to be in the final - a far sight from what was good in
terms of their rankings. Now, they have pretty much complete incentive to
do the best they can in a single game, which is what they're being ranked
by.

You can't perfectly mimic the incentive to do the best overall in a
tournament with the realm of a single game. And it's insane to try to
that within the realm of the entire tournament, as you once suggested.
(Dropouts and such will make the whole exercise arbitrary and silly.)
And in the process of trying either, you lose a lot of very valid results
within the context of a single game: when one player scores more VPs than
another player but does not win the game. That would be bad.

Fred

Easily enough fixed: Replace it with a 'scoring ratio' type number, like
1/50 (first in a 50-person tournament) or 4/20 (fourth in a 20-person
tournament). Just to satisfy my aesthetic of 'higher number = better
performance', mangle it by doing 1-(place/number of attendants), so
the guy who places 50th in a field of 50 has (1-(50/50))=0 averaged into
his lifetime place stat, and the guy who comes in third has (1-(3/50))=0.94.

So someone who wins every tournament they enter has a place stat of 1.00,
someone who loses every time has a stat of 0.00, and the rest of us
vary somewhere in between.

This stat can still be sandbagged by playing as many low-attendance
tournaments as possible, and doesn't reward winning a really big
event, but I don't feel these are huge vulnerabilities. Winning a big
event like a Gen*Con or French Championship tends to garner you a reputation
all by itself, anyway.
